corrected_value.title: Imperfect Public Monitoring with Costly Punishment: An Experimental Study

decisions.quote: Experimental Economics Replication Project Replication of Imperfect Public Monitoring with Costly Punishment: An Experimental Study by Ambrus, A. / Greiner, B. (2012) in: The American Economic Review, 102(7), 3317–3332 Replication Authors: Teck Hua Ho, Hang Wu Ambrus and Greiner conduct six treatments combining punishment severity and noise (imperfect monitoring) in sequential Prisoner’s Dilemma games. There is a surprising non-obvious U-shaped effect of severity on net earnings (earnings after paying punishment costs). Therefore, we will concentrate only on the basic effect of noise in the regular punishment condition. Hypothesis to bet on: When there is imperfect monitoring, allowing punishment reduces net earnings (i.e., earnings after punishment costs; a comparison of the regular punishment with noise treatment and the no punishment with noise treatment).
decisions.location: Primary Project Replication Report for Ambrus and Greiner (2012), page 1/3 (line 1282); Reference 34 (lines 288-289); Table S1 (line 1256)
decisions.reason: Both the shipped record and blind coding correctly identify the tested original study as Ambrus and Greiner (2012), 'Imperfect Public Monitoring with Costly Punishment: An Experimental Study', American Economic Review 102(7), 3317-3332 (Reference 34). The individual primary replication report and Table S1/S2 confirm that this specific published paper's finding on regular punishment under imperfect monitoring was directly re-tested.

decisions.quote: Replication Results In the replication study, when there is imperfect monitoring, allowing for regular punishment significantly reduces the net profits. This is consistent with the observation of the original study. Table 1 summarizes the results of ordinary least squares regressions of net earnings on the treatment dummy regular punishment and noise for the original and replication experiments. The treatment effect of −2.021 in the replication study is statistically significant with a p-value of 0.012 (t-test). Because of a lower standard error in the replication study the p-value is smaller compared to the original study (p-value of 0.057). As compared to the effect size of −2.914 in the original study, the relative effect size of the replication experiments equals 69.35% (−2.021/ − 2.914). 2/3 Experimental Economics Replication Project Unplanned Protocol Deviations Discussion The replication experiments were conducted exactly in the way as described above without any deviations from the protocol. Given the criteria and procedure outlined above, the hypothesis of interest has been replicated at a significance level of α < 5%. The relative effect size equals 69.35% and the p-value of the hypothesis test is 0.012.
decisions.location: Primary Project Replication Report for Ambrus and Greiner (2012), Replication Results and Discussion, pages 2/3-3/3 (line 1282); Table S1 (line 1256)
decisions.reason: The individual primary replication report for Ambrus and Greiner (2012) states an explicit overall replication verdict in the Discussion ('the hypothesis of interest has been replicated at a significance level of α < 5%'), with a significant negative effect of regular punishment under noise on net earnings (coefficient = -2.021, p = 0.012, relative effect size = 69.35%), corroborated by Table S1 ('Replicated: Yes'). Both shipped and blind correctly code the outcome as 'successful'.

decisions.quote: Differences from Original Study The replication procedure is identical to that of the original study, with some unavoidable deviations. This replication will be performed at National University of Singapore, in 2015, while the original data was gathered at the Australian School of Business Experimental Research Laboratory at the University of New South Wales in February and March 2010 and 2011. The experiment will be in English as in the original study.
decisions.location: Primary Project Replication Report for Ambrus and Greiner (2012), Differences from Original Study, page 2/3 (line 1282)
decisions.reason: The study collected new experimental data in a fresh sample of participants at the National University of Singapore in 2015 using the original z-Tree materials and instructions to re-test the published finding of Ambrus and Greiner (2012). Under the codebook, re-testing a previously published finding with new data in a different sample is a 'replication'.

corrected_value.title: The Lure of Authority: Motivation and Incentive Effects of Power

decisions.quote: Experimental Economics Replication Project Replication of The Lure of Authority: Motivation and Incentive Effects of Power by Fehr, E./Herz, H./Wilkening, T. (2013) in: The American Economic Review, 103(4), pp. 1325–1359 Replication Authors: Felix Holzmeister, Jürgen Huber, Michael Kirchler and Michael Razen Fehr et al. study an authority-delegation game and compare delegation when the principal cannot be overruled (high norec treatment) and when she can be overruled (phigh25 treatment). They find that the nonpecuniary disutility of being overruled causes a reluctance to delegate authority (there is more delegation in the high norec compared to the phigh25 treatment). Hypothesis to bet on: The nonpecuniary disutility of being overruled causes a reluctance to delegate authority (a comparison of the average delegation rate between the high norec and the phigh25 treatments).
decisions.location: Primary Project Replication Report for Fehr, Herz, and Wilkening (2013), page 1/3 (line 1317); Reference 42 (lines 305-306); Table S1 (line 1264)
decisions.reason: Both the shipped record and blind coding correctly identify the tested original study as Fehr, Herz, and Wilkening (2013), 'The Lure of Authority: Motivation and Incentive Effects of Power', American Economic Review 103(4), 1325-1359 (Reference 42). The individual primary replication report and Table S1/S2 confirm that this paper's between-subjects comparison of delegation rates (high norec vs. phigh25) was directly re-tested.

decisions.quote: A probit regression controlling for period fixed effects with standard errors clustered on the individual level yields a marginal effect coefficient, i.e. an effect size of 0.219 (see Table 1). This turns out to be statistically significant with a p-value of 0.026. Compared to the effect size of 0.262 in the original experiment, the relative effect size of the replication study equals 83.59% (0.219/0.262). Similar to the original study, the higher delegation rate in the high norec treatment occurred despite the fact that the empirical return on delegation is 15.15 percentage points higher in the phigh25 treatment than in high norec. Unplanned Protocol Deviations The replication experiments were conducted exactly in the way as described above without any deviations from the protocol. 2/3 Experimental Economics Replication Project Discussion Given the criteria and procedure outlined above, the hypothesis of interest has been replicated at a significance level of α < 5%. The relative effect size equals 83.59% and the p-value of the hypothesis test is 0.026.
decisions.location: Primary Project Replication Report for Fehr, Herz, and Wilkening (2013), Replication Results and Discussion, pages 2/3-3/3 (line 1317); Table S1 (line 1264)
decisions.reason: The individual primary replication report for Fehr, Herz, and Wilkening (2013) states an explicit overall verdict in the Discussion ('the hypothesis of interest has been replicated at a significance level of α < 5%'), finding a significantly higher delegation rate in the high norec treatment than in the phigh25 treatment (64.67% vs. 43.11%, marginal effect = 0.219, p = 0.026, relative effect size = 83.59%), corroborated by Table S1 ('Replicated: Yes'). Both shipped and blind correctly code the outcome as 'successful'.

decisions.quote: Differences from Original Study The replication procedure is identical to that of the original study, with some unavoidable deviations. This replication will be performed at the University of Innsbruck, Austria, in 2015, on students from the University of Innsbruck, while the original data was gathered at Zurich University, Switzerland, in 2011, with students from Zurich University and the Federal Institute of Technology in Zurich. The experiment will be conducted in German as the original study. The paper studies a number of treatments. For replication, the focus is only on the comparison between high norec and phigh25. We have chosen this hypothesis because we think it is the main between-subjects treatment comparison in the paper.
decisions.location: Primary Project Replication Report for Fehr, Herz, and Wilkening (2013), Differences from Original Study, page 2/3 (line 1317)
decisions.reason: The study collected new experimental data from a fresh sample of 102 students at the University of Innsbruck in 2015 (versus the original 2011 sample at Zurich University and ETH Zurich) to re-test the published finding of Fehr, Herz, and Wilkening (2013). Under the codebook, re-testing a previously published finding with new data in a different sample is a 'replication'.
